title: नागरिक–सैनिक सम्बन्धः वर्तमान अवस्था, चुनौती र अवसर Nagarik- Sainik Sambandha: Bartaman Awastha, Chunauti ra Abasar
nepali: राष्ट्रिय सुरक्षाका मामिलामा मात्र होइन संबिधान रलोकतन्त्रको रक्षाका लागि देशको सेनाको भूमिका पनित्यत्तिकै महŒवपूर्ण हुन्छ भने देशको शान्ति, स्थायित्व,समग्र बिकास र सम्वृद्धि तथा देशको वैदेशिक नीतिर कूटनीतिमा समेत सेनाले महŒवपूर्ण योगदानदिन सक्छ । तर यसका लागि सबल र प्रभावकारीनागरिक–सैनिक सम्बन्धको आबश्यकता पर्दछ ।  नागरिक–सैनिक सम्बन्धलाई प्रभाबकारी बनाउन एकातिर देशको नागरिक नेतृत्व, नागरिक समाजर कर्मचारीतन्त्रमा सुरक्षासम्बन्धी पर्याप्त ज्ञान रअनुभव हुनु आबश्यक छ भने अर्कोतिर उत्तरदायित्वर जबाफदेहिताका हिसाबले सेनाको तालिम र नेतृत्वबिकासस“गै नागरिक नेतृत्वको वैध र न्यायसंगत आदेशअक्षरश ः पालना गर्नुपर्छ भन्ने मान्यता स्थापित हुनुजरुरी छ । यसका अतिरिक्त नागरिक र सैनिक नेतृत्वबिचको नियमित संबाद र सह–कार्यको त्यत्तिकै महŒव हुन्छ भने सुरक्षाबारे संवेदनशील कुरा बाहेक सेनाको नियमित काम–कार्बाही, सैनिक बजेट, खर्च र कोष परिचालनआदिमा पारदर्शिता बढाउने काम गरे तथा सेनाभित्रदण्डहीनता छ भन्ने आरोपलाई सम्बोधन गर्न नेपालीसेनाले बिश्वब्यापी मान्यतालाई आत्मसात् गरे आम–नागरिकमा सेनाप्रति विश्वास र भरोसा अझै बढ्नेछ ।  सेनापति पूर्णचन्द्र थापाको नेतृत्वमा सेनामा सुशासन रसुधारका कार्यक्रम सुरु हुनु आफै“मा सराहनीय छ र यीसुधारहरूलाई सेनाको भाबी नेतृत्व बिकासस“ग जोडेर संस्थागत गर्नुपर्छ, किनकि सेनाको लोकतान्त्रीकरण  भन्नाले नागरिक नेतृत्वको नियन्त्रणका अतिरिक्त सेनाको व्यावसायिक बिकास अनि सेनामा सुशासन र सुधारप्रतिको प्रतिबद्धता हो भनेर बुझ्नुपर्ने हुन्छ ।  नेपालको राष्ट्रिय सुरक्षाको संरचनात्मक सुधारकाकुरा गर्दा अमेरिका र भारतमा जस्तै राष्ट्रिय सुरक्षापरिषद्को पुन ः संरचना गरेर नीतिगत, व्यावसायिक रसंयोजनकारी क्षमता बढाउनु जरुरी छ ।
american_english: The role of the country's army is equally important not only in matters of national security but also in the defense of the constitution and democracy, and the army can make a significant contribution to the country's peace, stability, overall development and prosperity, as well as to the country's foreign policy and diplomacy. But for this, a strong and effective civil–military relationship is needed. To make civil–military relations effective, on the one hand the country's civilian leadership, civil society and civil service must have adequate knowledge and experience of security, while on the other hand the conviction must be established that, in terms of responsibility and accountability, the legitimate and just orders of the civilian leadership must be followed to the letter, together with the army's training and leadership development. In addition to this, regular dialogue and cooperation between the civilian and military leadership are equally important, and if, apart from sensitive matters concerning security, work is done to increase transparency in the army's regular operations, military budget, expenditure and fund mobilization and so on, and if the Nepali Army embraces universal norms in order to address the charge that there is impunity within the army, trust and confidence in the army among ordinary citizens will grow further. The start of good-governance and reform programs in the army under the leadership of Chief of Army Staff Purna Chandra Thapa is in itself commendable, and these reforms must be institutionalized by linking them to the development of the army's future leadership, because the democratization of the army must be understood as meaning, in addition to civilian control, the army's professional development and a commitment to good governance and reform within the army. When speaking of structural reform of Nepal's national security, it is necessary to restructure the National Security Council as in the United States and India and to enhance its policy, professional and coordination capacities.
british_english: The role of the country's army is equally important not only in matters of national security but also in the defence of the constitution and democracy, while the army can make a significant contribution to the country's peace, stability, overall development and prosperity, and also to the country's foreign policy and diplomacy. Yet for this a robust and effective relationship between civilians and the military is required. To make civil–military relations effective, it is necessary on the one hand that the country's civilian leadership, civil society and civil service possess sufficient knowledge and experience of security, and on the other that the belief be established that, in terms of responsibility and accountability, the legitimate and just orders of the civilian leadership must be obeyed to the letter, alongside the army's training and leadership development. Beyond this, regular dialogue and co-operation between the civilian and military leadership are of equal importance, and should steps be taken — apart from sensitive matters concerning security — to widen transparency in the army's routine business, the military budget, expenditure and fund mobilisation and so forth, and should the Nepali Army take on board universal norms in order to answer the allegation that there is impunity inside the army, then trust and confidence in the army among the general public will grow yet further. That good-governance and reform programmes have begun in the army under the leadership of the Chief of Army Staff, Purna Chandra Thapa, is in itself praiseworthy, and these reforms must needs be institutionalised by tying them to the development of the army's future leadership, since the democratisation of the army has to be understood as meaning, over and above civilian control, the army's professional development and a commitment to good governance and reform in the army. In speaking of structural reform of Nepal's national security, it is essential to reconstitute the National Security Council as in America and India and to strengthen its policy, professional and coordinating capacities.
australian_english: The army's role counts just as much not only in national security matters but also in defending the constitution and democracy, and the army can make a solid contribution to the country's peace, stability, overall development and prosperity, and to its foreign policy and diplomacy too. But you need a strong, effective civil–military relationship for that. To get civil–military relations working, on the one side the country's civilian leadership, civil society and public service need enough know-how and experience of security, and on the other the idea has to take hold that, when it comes to responsibility and accountability, the civilian leadership's legitimate and fair orders have to be followed to the letter, along with the army's training and leadership development. On top of that, regular talk and co-operation between the civilian and military leadership matter just as much, and if, leaving aside sensitive security matters, they lift transparency in the army's regular operations, the military budget, spending and fund mobilisation and the like, and if the Nepali Army takes on universal norms to deal with the claim that there's impunity inside the army, then trust and confidence in the army among ordinary citizens will grow further again. The fact that good-governance and reform programmes have got going in the army under Chief of Army Staff Purna Chandra Thapa is commendable in itself, and these reforms have to be locked in institutionally by tying them to the development of the army's future leadership, because democratising the army has to be understood as meaning, beyond civilian control, the army's professional development and a commitment to good governance and reform within the army. When it comes to structural reform of Nepal's national security, there's a real need to restructure the National Security Council the way they do in the US and India and build up its policy, professional and coordination capacity.
